items.title: Supporting Ergonomic Risk Assessment: An AI-driven Approach for Action Recognition Using Standard Video Recordings
items.abstract: Background: While AI has been widely adopted in medical, social, and industrial fields, its use in ergonomic risk assessment of occupational movements is limited. Existing automated activity recognition methods often rely on controlled conditions or extra sensors, reducing their practicality. This study aims to develop an AI-driven tool to digitize the Occupational Repetitive Actions (OCRA) risk assessment by automatically identifying occupational actions from standard video recordings in real manufacturing settings. The goal is to help ergonomists conduct risk assessments more broadly and support workers’ health. Methods: Video data were collected from 37 workstations across multiple manufacturing facilities, comprising 869 action clips representing 12 distinct occupational activities. Two-dimensional skeletal pose extraction was performed using MMAction2 to anonymize workers and reduce environmental confounding factors. Graph Convolutional Network architectures (ST-GCN and Two-Stream Adaptive GCN) were trained and validated using stratified dataset partitioning (67.3% training, 24.7% validation, 8.0% test). Results: The proposed model achieved approximately 60% classification accuracy, substantially outperforming the frequency-based (12%) and duration-based (24%) baselines. The performance evaluation used multiple metrics, including Mean Average Precision, F1-score, Jaccard/IoU, Dice-Sørensen coefficient, and Hausdorff distance. Conclusions: This work demonstrates the technical feasibility of AI-driven, markerless motion capture systems for digitalizing musculoskeletal disorder risk assessment in real-world occupational settings. The principal innovation is the successful implementation of action recognition from standard video recordings captured in uncontrolled manufacturing environments, which transcends spatial constraints and eliminates the need for specialized sensing equipment. Despite current limitations in dataset size and classification accuracy, this study lays a foundation for developing deployable platforms to support real-time ergonomic assessment and proactive prevention of work-related musculoskeletal disorders.

items.title: Survivability Engineering for Future Defense Systems: A System-Level Framework for Mission Continuity, Adaptability, Recoverability, and Operational Effectiveness
items.abstract: Rapid technological change is altering the conditions under which defense systems are designed, evaluated, and sustained. Advances in autonomous systems, electronic warfare, artificial intelligence, precision technologies, sensing, and digital engineering are occurring alongside increasingly rapid cycles of countermeasure development and operational adaptation. Within this environment, conventional protection-centered approaches provide an incomplete basis for evaluating system effectiveness. A platform may withstand physical damage yet lose mobility, communication, navigation, sensing, or another mission-critical function; conversely, a degraded system may retain sufficient capability to continue contributing to mission objectives. These conditions require a broader engineering perspective centered on the preservation of operational value rather than physical survival alone. This article develops survivability engineering as a system-level framework integrating protection, mobility, endurance, mission continuity, adaptability, recoverability, operational availability, communication resilience, electronic warfare resilience, signature management, autonomy, and mission effectiveness. Particular attention is given to mission continuity as a governing design objective and to adaptability and recoverability as lifecycle characteristics of future defense systems. The framework is examined across human, land, unmanned, naval, aerospace, and critical-infrastructure domains to demonstrate how survivability requirements vary by platform while retaining a common system-level logic. The study further considers modularity, redundancy, maintainability, digital engineering, simulation, operational feedback, and continuous modernization as mechanisms through which survivability can be sustained as threats and technologies evolve. Rather than treating survivability as an extension of armor or physical protection, the article positions survivability engineering as a continuous multidisciplinary process linking design, manufacturing, sustainment, modernization, and operational learning. This perspective provides a foundation for evaluating future defense systems according to their ability to preserve mission effectiveness under disruption, degradation, uncertainty, and technological change.

items.abstract: To deal with environmental loss and over-tourism, the global tourism industry is shifting to value-based, sustainable and resilient paradigms, rather than mass-market consumption. It proposes a socio-technical model named Digital Resilient Placemaking, that makes use of high-fidelity 3D models and geospatial information One of the core approaches of this model is Virtual Offloading or preventative tourismThe framework employs the use of Edge-AI to provide low-latency interactions in order to make these experiences seamless and contextually aware, which is especially important to maintain some intangible cultural heritage, such as oral traditions. The study uses behavioral psychology to quantify the Flow Experience and Psychological Capital of travellers as well. This framework can enable local stakeholders to leverage human-AI interaction to spur economic resilience by upgrading the automated brochures to autonomous interactive environments

items.title: Sycophancy y recompensa: el acuerdo con el usuario no es la corrección / Sycophancy and reward: agreeing with the user is not being correct
items.abstract: Que un asistente dé la razón a quien le pregunta se cuenta a menudo como un solo fenómeno con una sola causa: la optimización de la preferencia humana. Este artículo separa tres evidencias que comparten el síntoma. La primera es la sycophancy medida con protocolo: el cambio de respuesta al añadir la opinión o el desafío del usuario, frente a un control del mismo diseño. Con ese protocolo, sugerir una respuesta incorrecta reduce la accuracy hasta un 27 % en LLaMA 2, y Claude 1.3 admite un error no cometido en el 98 % de las preguntas; en un estudio de 2025 con tres modelos de API, el 58,19 % de los casos cambia ante una réplica, pero solo el 14,66 % se aleja de lo correcto. La segunda es la sobreoptimización: seguir optimizando contra un modelo de recompensa degrada un proxy de calidad —la puntuación de otro modelo de recompensa o un win rate de resúmenes—, y ningún eje de esas curvas es sycophancy. La tercera es el comunicado con el que OpenAI retiró en abril de 2025 una actualización de GPT-4o por aduladora, sin publicar la cifra de tráfico afectado. La hipótesis causal sobre la preferencia tiene apoyo parcial: el preference model de Claude 2 prefiere la respuesta aduladora a una corrección breve el 95 % de las veces en 266 misconceptions, pero optimizar contra él baja unas formas de sycophancy y sube otras. La contraevidencia incluye un piloto sin sycophancy significativa en ChatGPT y Bard, un finetuning que la reduce sin pérdida apreciable en benchmarks y un estudio que atribuye la deferencia al registro más que a la credencial. La contribución es un ledger por afirmación, una tabla de protocolos y la distinción entre acuerdo instrumental y acuerdo epistémico, que las fuentes separan como norma pero no como umbral medido. English abstract: That an assistant agrees with whoever asks is often told as a single phenomenon with a single cause: the optimisation of human preference. This paper separates three kinds of evidence that share the symptom. The first is sycophancy measured with a protocol: the change of answer when the user's opinion or challenge is added, against a control of the same design. With that protocol, suggesting an incorrect answer reduces accuracy by up to 27% in LLaMA 2, and Claude 1.3 admits a mistake it did not make on 98% of questions; in a 2025 study of three API models, 58.19% of cases change after a rebuttal, but only 14.66% move away from the correct answer. The second is overoptimisation: continuing to optimise against a reward model degrades a proxy of quality—the score of another reward model, or a summarisation win rate—and no axis of those curves is sycophancy. The third is the statement with which OpenAI rolled back a GPT-4o update in April 2025 for being sycophantic, without publishing the figure for the traffic affected. The causal hypothesis about preference has partial support: the Claude 2 preference model prefers the sycophantic response to a brief correction 95% of the time over 266 misconceptions, but optimising against it lowers some forms of sycophancy and raises others. The counter-evidence includes a pilot with no significant sycophancy in ChatGPT and Bard, a finetuning that reduces it with no appreciable benchmark loss, and a study that attributes deference to register more than to credentials. The contribution is a claim-by-claim ledger, a table of protocols and the distinction between instrumental and epistemic agreement, which the sources separate as norms but not as a measured threshold. Working paper de la serie WHITE-PAPERS (wp-2026-038, v0.9). Incluye versión en español e inglés. No revisado por pares. Uso de herramientas de IA declarado en el manuscrito; sin conflictos de interés ni financiación.

items.title: Synthetic Future
items.abstract: There is no single static future, only a range of possible ones, and this closing chapter surveys the paths that lie ahead. It follows the “death of the author” to its logical endpoint, in which apparent democratization of creativity threatens the knowledge exchange while the access to high-quality sources might land behind paywalls. It also asks what currencies, including computing power, attention, and data, we will pay with for this new world. Machine consciousness remains a distant but possibly relevant question; however, there is far more urgent problem of human unconsciousness: our failure to grasp what deepening immersion in synthetic relationships, deeply emotional exchanges with chatbots, and AI companionship is already doing to us. Visiting Moltbook, an experimental social network built entirely for AI agents, and revisiting Cory Doctorow’s theory of enshittification applied to humanoid robots, this chapter weighs pessimistic and hopeful scenarios side by side, from a “Made by Human” backlash prizing authenticity to a call for “competencies for the future” we collectively lack: critical thinking, attentiveness, and the refusal to outsource judgment and decision-making entirely to algorithms.

items.title: Synthetic Labor
items.abstract: The rise of AI has reignited century-old fears about technological unemployment, echoing the anxieties of the nineteenth-century Luddites. This chapter revisits their history, challenging the simplistic narrative that casts critics of automation as mere enemies of progress, and traces a parallel through Pope Leo XIV’s warnings about a new “technofeudalism” threatening human dignity and labor rights. The author examines how generative AI is reshaping the labor market – to the paradoxical revival of manual trades as white-collar work grows automatable – and asks what becomes of productivity, creativity, and status once algorithms can perform many cognitive tasks. Turning to the creative sphere, this chapter explores AI-generated music, art, and virtual idols. The collapse of Kraków’s Off Radio experiment, where AI hosts briefly replaced human journalists, illustrates both the promise and backlash surrounding such transitions.

items.title: Synthetic Relationships
items.abstract: In an era increasingly described as an “epidemic of loneliness,” AI promises companionship on demand. This chapter traces how synthetic relationships have moved from novelty to mass phenomenon, opening with Yurina Noguchi, a Japanese woman who held a symbolic wedding ceremony with her ChatGPT partner, and widening out to the booming industry of AI companions apps. They serve millions of users, many of them teenagers, to form attachments regularly deeper than human friendships. The author examines the psychological mechanisms, from anthropomorphization to cognitive dissonance, behind these bonds, and confronts unsettling cases, including AI toys that discuss weapons and sex habits with children, and a robot companion mourned by a six-year-old. A closing section turns to so-called “sycophancy,” the tendency of chatbots to flatter and agree with users at the expense of honesty, revealing why systems built to please may be the worst possible substitute for real human connection.

items.title: Synthetic Therapy
items.abstract: As access to mental health services remains limited and expensive, many people are turning to chatbots as substitutes for psychotherapy. This chapter follows Jodie, a woman who has spent ten months treating ChatGPT as her therapist, to explore why synthetic conversation feels so convincing. Large language model is always available, never judges, and never grows tired. The author discusses the question of consciousness – both on chatbot’s and patients’ side – and traces back the discussion to Blake Lemoine, the Google engineer who believed his chatbot had become conscious. This chapter discusses the first psychological breakthroughs based on the research conducted by Joseph Weizenbaum in the 1960s. His ELIZA was able to make users trust a simple script. At the center of this chapter lies “sycophancy,” the tendency of chatbots to flatter and validate rather than challenge, which can shade into something more dangerous when users mistake fluent mechanical agreement for genuine understanding, and treat chatbot’s responses as divine or revealed. This chapter closes with the hardest material in this book: lawsuits alleging that AI chatbots encouraged vulnerable teenagers toward suicide, forcing an uncomfortable question about what happens when synthetic companionship fills a void that real human connection failed to reach.

items.title: Teacher Mediation of AI Use and Learning Autonomy at SMP Negeri 4 Pekanbaru
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) expands access to information and instructional support while raising concerns about information accuracy, cognitive dependence, and learning autonomy. This study examines how teachers mediate AI use while strengthening students’ independent learning at SMP Negeri 4 Pekanbaru. A qualitative case study was conducted in August 2026 with five purposively selected informants: one school principal, three subject teachers, and one Grade VIII student. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and supporting documentation and analyzed using thematic analysis. The findings reveal several interconnected patterns: AI functions as a learning assistant; teachers validate AI-generated information; structured tasks maintain students’ cognitive engagement; digital-device use is regulated according to instructional purposes; and teachers increasingly act as facilitators, mentors, validators, learning designers, and technology regulators. The study proposes a teacher-mediated AI balance in which access to AI is followed by teacher guidance, verification, independent processing, and learner accountability. This pattern offers a practical framework for integrating AI while sustaining reasoning, responsibility, and self-regulated learning in junior secondary education.

items.title: Teachers' artificial intelligence self-efficacy: development and validation of a multidimensional scale grounded in social cognitive theory
items.abstract: Introduction As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in education, it is important to know how confident teachers feel about using it. Research has examined AI literacy, AI readiness and AI competency, yet few validated instruments measure teachers' AI self-efficacy specifically. The aim of this study was to develop and validate the Artificial Intelligence Self-Efficacy Scale for Teachers (AISES-T). Methods Data were collected from teachers in different regions of Turkiye within a scale development design. Following expert review, a pool of 50 items was reduced to a 27-item trial form. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) using principal axis factoring was conducted in a first sample of 313 teachers, and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was conducted in a second, independent sample of 559 teachers. Results The EFA yielded 22 items in three factors — AI Use and Learning Self-Efficacy (11 items), Pedagogical AI Integration Self-Efficacy (7 items) and AI Awareness and Understanding Self-Efficacy (4 items) — explaining 68.51% of the variance. The CFA supported the three-factor model, χ 2 (194) = 681.49, p < 0.001, χ 2 /df = 3.51, RMSEA = 0.067 (90% CI [0.062, 0.073]), SRMR = 0.044, CFI = 0.956, IFI = 0.956, TLI = 0.948, which fitted considerably better than a one-factor model, Δ χ 2 (3) = 2,202.35, p < 0.001. Cronbach's α coefficients were 0.92–0.96 for the subscales and 0.96 for the whole scale, and composite reliability ranged from 0.92 to 0.95. Standardized loadings (0.645–0.917) and average variance extracted (AVE = 0.609–0.730) supported convergent validity, while the Fornell-Larcker criterion and heterotrait-monotrait ratios (0.632–0.776) supported discriminant validity. Discussion The results show that teachers' AI self-efficacy comprises related but distinguishable beliefs about learning with AI, integrating it into instruction and understanding how it works. The AISES-T offers a valid and reliable measure for research on AI-supported teaching and for planning teacher professional development.

items.title: Teachers’ experiences with generative AI for lesson planning: A qualitative study in Sindh, Pakistan
items.abstract: This Qualitative descriptive study explored how 15 in service Junior Elementary School teachers (JESTs) at Government Higher Secondary School Dad Laghari, Sindh, Pakistan, described their familiarity and use of artificial intelligence (GenAI) for lesson planning, perceived benefits and challenges, and professional learning and support needs. Participants provided written English responses to five open ended questions and profile information. Responses were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis and participant characteristics were summarized descriptively. From the study five themes were identified like Familiarity with GenAI and reported planning uses; perceived efficiency and expanded planning options; verification of generated materials for accuracy and classroom fit; integration of AI fluency with subject and pedagogical knowledge ; and collegial and institutional support. Teachers reported using GenAI to draft lesson notes, questions, activities, examples, and explanations. Thirteen reported frequent use, while two reported occasional use. Participants showed concerns about accuracy, curriculum and learner suitability, privacy and internet access and identified need for practical training, peer exchange, digital resources and school guidance. The findings highlights self reported perspective from one school; lesson plan, classroom practice and student outcomes were not assessed.

items.title: Teaching at the Crossroads
items.abstract: This chapter explores a seasoned educator’s perspective on the constructive role of artificial intelligence in graduate art therapy education. Drawing from her experiences developing a personal AI policy and integrating AI tools into course assignments, the author examines both the pedagogical benefits and students’ responses to these innovations. Grounded in contemporary scholarship on emerging best practices in higher education and the growing literature on AI within art therapy training and clinical practice, the chapter argues that AI literacy constitutes an essential component of the hidden curriculum in therapist education. The author also presents exploratory exercises co-created with AI to help students identify common errors in AI generated research and to support critical engagement with developing technologies.

items.title: The Algorithm Is a Woman: How Feminized Futures Are Coded into Precarity and Promise
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is commonly presented as neutral, autonomous, and future-oriented, yet its interfaces, narratives, and labor infrastructures remain shaped by older gendered expectations. This article advances a new account of AI feminization by connecting symbolic representation to the material organization of hidden labor. Using a mixed-methods design, the study combines interface analysis of fifteen widely used AI systems, critical discourse analysis of 500 public and industry artifacts published between 2018 and 2026, and critical infrastructural document analysis of job advertisements, contractor records, technical reports, model cards, labor documents, and workplace policies. The findings show that AI systems repeatedly perform feminized qualities such as care, patience, emotional responsiveness, availability, and service, while the labor producing these qualities is distributed across annotators, moderators, evaluators, and quality-assurance workers whose contributions remain obscured. The study further demonstrates that AI’s promises of empowerment and efficiency coexist with contractual precarity, surveillance, emotional burden, and unequal global value extraction. By theorizing AI as feminized in interface, discourse, and infrastructure, the article reveals algorithmic intelligence as a social relation rather than a technical achievement. More equitable AI futures therefore require labor visibility, accountability, worker protection, and infrastructural justice.

items.title: The Algorithmic Leviathan: A PESTEL Analysis of Power, Autonomy, and Franchise in the Epoch of Artificial General Intelligence
items.abstract: This article examines how the progressive rollout of artificial intelligence, and prospectively artificial general intelligence (AGI), alters the equation between institutional power, human autonomy, individual agency and the democratic franchise. Treating AI as a "bureaucratic native" that realises the Weberian ideal of rule-bound, impersonal administration, it traces the shift of discretion from street-level to system-level and algorithmic bureaucracy, and then applies a PESTEL (Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, Legal) analysis. The political section argues for traceable audit trails over civic registries; the economic section offers a stylised illustration of the human labour share and contrasts Universal Basic Income with Universal Basic Capital; the social section draws on the Dutch SyRI judgment and the Rotterdam welfare-algorithm case; and the environmental and legal sections address the compute–energy trilemma, the GDPR, the EU AI Act as amended by the AI Omnibus, and Council of Europe Convention CETS No. 225. Three comparative tables and five figures summarise the argument. The article concludes that the distribution of power in the AGI epoch will be determined less by the capability of the technology than by the legal, economic and institutional choices that encode meaningful human oversight, explanation and appeal. **Keywords:** artificial general intelligence; PESTEL; algorithmic bureaucracy; artificial discretion; algorithmic due process; audit trails; labour share; Universal Basic Capital; data centres; EU AI Act; GDPR; CETS 225; KSCCN

items.title: The Application of Self-Determination Theory to Short-form Video Addiction: The Roles of Psychological Needs and Intrinsic Motivations
items.abstract: Short-form video applications are widely used worldwide. At the same time, new concerns have been raised owing to excessive and addictive short-form video use, with significant harm to health and well-being. By self-determination theory, the present study aimed to test the effects of satisfaction and frustration of three basic psychological needs (autonomy, competence, and relatedness) in relation to short-form video addiction (SVA) and evaluate the roles of the intrinsic motivations for passing time and entertainment underlying such relationships. The study included 367 Chinese TikTok users (37.1% male) aged 18 to 62 years ( M ± SD = 20.63 ± 4.40 years), who voluntarily completed an anonymous online questionnaire without compensation. All three types of need satisfaction had significant negative associations with SVA, while the three types of need frustration were significantly positively associated with SVA. Entertainment motivation significantly and negatively mediated the relationship between competence/relatedness satisfaction and SVA while significantly and positively mediating the relationship between relatedness frustration and SVA. Motivation for passing time served as a risk-enhancing mediator in the relationship between competence/relatedness frustration and SVA. Therefore, this study identified relatedness frustration and motivation for passing time as the most salient risk factors of SVA. The implications for SVA interventions that focus on psychological needs and intrinsic motivation are also discussed.

items.title: The ChatGPT source cue shapes answer acceptance in a reasoning task
items.abstract: Introduction As generative AI systems increasingly provide answers in everyday and academic contexts, understanding how source attribution influences evaluative judgment has become critical. Methods In a within-subjects design, 103 participants evaluated 30 pre-generated reflective-correct, intuitive-incorrect, and arithmetic control-correct answers labeled ChatGPT or computer. Assignment of two parallel batteries to source labels and trial presentation order were randomized, and displays were visually matched. An independent unlabeled pretest with 35 participants supported battery comparability. Results Participant-level analysis showed greater overall acceptance under ChatGPT (68.0% versus 63.4%, p = 0.002). A trial-level logistic mixed model with crossed participant and parallel-problem-pair random intercepts showed a source-by-category interaction ( p < 0.001): acceptance was higher under ChatGPT for arithmetic controls (OR = 6.08, 95% CI [2.70, 13.69]), while source contrasts within the two CRT categories were not significant. Judgment accuracy is reported descriptively. Signal-detection analyses of CRT answers detected no significant source difference in sensitivity ( p = 0.930) or criterion ( p = 0.082). Evaluation times were longer under ChatGPT in the raw-time analysis ( p = 0.034), but the source difference was not significant after log transformation ( p = 0.180). Exploratory correlations detected no significant associations between source-related differences and trust, AI attitudes, or critical-thinking disposition. Discussion These findings distinguish overall source-related endorsement, particularly for arithmetic controls, from successful discrimination between correct and incorrect CRT answers.

items.title: The Dual Nature of AI-Supported Medical Decision-Making: A Conceptual Framework of Efficiency, Responsibility, and Human–AI Collaboration
items.abstract: In the medical field, while AI-driven systems promise enhanced efficiency, diagnostic accuracy, and operational effectiveness, they also raise critical concerns about responsibility, accountability, and ethical judgment. Despite the growing body of empirical research on medical AI, limited attention has been given to the theoretical implications of AI integration from a management and organizational perspective. Our study develops a conceptual framework to explain the dual nature of AI-supported medical decision-making by integrating insights from decision-making theory, algorithmic management, and healthcare management literature. We propose that AI simultaneously enhances decision efficiency while creating new forms of responsibility ambiguity and ethical tension. The framework conceptualizes how AI capability, human–AI interaction, and organizational governance jointly shape decision outcomes, professional accountability, and organizational trust. By offering a theoretically grounded model, this study contributes to literature in three ways. First, it extends traditional decision-making theory to AI-augmented healthcare contexts. Second, it introduces responsibility as a central construct in human–AI collaboration. Third, it provides a foundation for future empirical research and managerial practice in healthcare organizations navigating AI adoption.

items.title: The Engineering-Oriented Empirical Turn in the Philosophy of Technology and AI: Perspectives from American and Chinese Pragmatism
items.abstract: This article critically interrogates the analytical historiography of the engineering-oriented “empirical turn” in the philosophy of technology and artificial intelligence (AI) by contrasting the accounts of Hans Achterhuis, Philip Brey, and Vincent Blok with the pragmatist frameworks of Stephen H. Cutcliffe and Bocong Li. While Achterhuis institutionalized the “American philosophy of technology: empirical turn” and Brey theorized this paradigm through Carl Mitcham’s humanities-vs.-engineering dichotomy, their strictly analytical orientation significantly disregards both American and Chinese pragmatist traditions. To bridge this conceptual omission, this study operationalizes Cutcliffe’s and Li’s engineering philosophies by integrating Charles Sanders Peirce’s nominalism and experimentalism, William James’s consequentialism, and medieval Muslim philosopher al-Ghazâlî’s nominalist-experimentalist insights. We position Cutcliffe and Li as the foundational theorists of American and Chinese pragmatist engineering-oriented empirical turns, respectively, both arguing that the discipline must be fundamentally rooted in society-centered, generative production processes—a stance that directly challenges Brey’s taxonomies. Furthermore, although the “philosophy of AI” emerged through the seminal works of Margaret A. Boden (1990) and Matt Carter (2007), this article substantiates why the discourse must now be subsumed under a broader philosophy of technology. Ultimately, by leveraging Li’s ontology—which aligns technological production with historical identity and existential validation—this article synthesizes an engineering-oriented empirical paradigm with contemporary post-colonial manufacturing and technological agency.

items.title: The Impact Of Artificial Intelligence Technologies in Recent Years on the Work Environment in Riyadh
items.abstract: AbstractObjective: This study aimed to identify the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, specifically machine learning, natural language processing, intelligent robots, and decision support systems, on the work environment of organizations operating in Riyadh.Methodology: The study employed a descriptive-analytical approach. The study population consisted of employees working in organizations implementing AI technologies in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. A simple random sample of 394 employees was used, and an electronic questionnaire was the primary data collection tool.Results: The study found a high level of AI technology implementation in Riyadh organizations, with a mean score of 4.06. The quality of the work environment was also found to be high, with a mean score of 4.01. A statistically significant effect of AI technologies on the work environment was found at the 0.01 level, with the dimensions collectively explaining 70.8% of the variance in the dependent variable. The "decision support systems" dimension demonstrated the greatest impact.Recommendations: The study recommended enhancing investment in digital infrastructure, designing specialized training programs, expanding the application of decision support systems, and establishing a legislative and ethical framework that regulates the use of these technologies in work environments.

items.title: The Impact of Geographic Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI) Applications on Enhancing the Efficiency of Executive Decision-Making: An Applied Study of National Water Company Projects in the Southern Region
items.abstract: AbstractObjective: The study aimed to reveal the impact of using Geographic Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI) applications on the efficiency of executive decision-making in the National Water Company’s projects in the southern region, through studying four main dimensions: collection and processing of smart spatial data, predictive spatial analysis, spatial visualization and decision support, and operational integration with project management. The study also examined the extent to which these applications reflect on the quality of decisions made and the speed of response to problems related to implementation.Methodology: The study followed the descriptive analytical approach. The study population consisted of employees related to the fields of operation and maintenance, digital transformation, and geographic information systems, in addition to employees in the administrative and technical fields of the company under study. The purposive sampling method was followed, and the study sample amounted to (34) employees from the National Water Company in the Southern Region. The questionnaire was used as the primary tool for collecting data.Results: The results showed that the level of use of geographic artificial intelligence applications was very high, with an arithmetic mean of (4.39). The efficiency of executive decision-making was also very high, with an average of (4.47). The average quality of decision and executive response was (4.62). The results proved the existence of a strong and statistically significant positive relationship between the use of GeoAI applications and the efficiency of executive decision-making. It was shown that there was a statistically significant effect of geographic artificial intelligence (GeoAI) applications on the efficiency of executive decision-making in the projects of the National Water Company in the Southern Region, as the applications explained about (79.7%) of the variance in decision efficiency.Recommendations: The study recommended expanding the use of predictive spatial analysis, developing a unified spatial platform, enhancing integration between GeoAI and project management, operation and maintenance systems, along with training staff and establishing a clear framework for data governance and intelligent models.

items.title: The Impact of Healthcare Cost Management on Operational Efficiency in Diagnostic Radiology Departments: A field study in Public Hospitals in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia
items.abstract: AbstractObjective: This study aimed to identify the impact of healthcare cost management in its four dimensions (cost planning, cost control, cost analysis, and cost reduction) on operational efficiency in diagnostic radiology departments in public hospitals in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Methodology: The study adopted the descriptive analytical approach. The study population consisted of all employees in the financial, accounting, administrative and technical departments associated with the diagnostic radiology departments in the public hospitals affiliated with the Ministry of Health in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. The simple random sampling method was adopted, and the questionnaire tool was adopted, as it was distributed to (380) individuals from the employees in the financial, accounting and technical departments associated with the radiology departments in the public hospitals in the five main administrative regions of the Kingdom. (328) questionnaires were returned that were valid for statistical analysis at a rate of (86.32%).Results: The study found a substantial and direct relationship between health cost management and operational efficiency in diagnostic radiology departments in public hospitals in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, positive and statistically significant at the level of (0.01). It also showed a statistically significant positive effect at the significance level of (0.05) of health cost management with its combined dimensions on operational efficiency, as the coefficient of determination reached a value of (0.709), meaning that the dimensions of cost management explain (70.9%) of the variance in operational efficiency. The dimensions of health cost management in their impact on operational efficiency were ranked in descending order as follows: cost control, then cost analysis, then cost planning, and finally cost reduction.Recommendations: The study recommended the need to adopt modern methods in cost management such as activity-based costing (ABC) and target costing, employ artificial intelligence techniques and business intelligence tools, enhance cost control through specialized units for analyzing deviations, and develop the quality system in diagnostic radiology departments.

items.title: The impact of LLM-based recommendations on decisions under uncertainty
items.abstract: Abstract We study how large language model (LLM) based recommendations affect evaluations of uncertainty. We elicit certainty equivalents for (i) lotteries that share the same reduced-form winning probability but vary in cognitive demands because they are compound, and (ii) an Ellsberg-style ambiguous lottery. Across all lottery types, valuations from participants who receive LLM-based recommendations before each valuation exhibit second-order stochastic dominance relative to valuations from participants who do not. Hence, LLM-based recommendations leave mean valuations unchanged but compress the distribution, reducing the incidence of extreme valuations. Consistent with this pattern, LLM-based recommendations reduce the intensity of risk, complexity, and ambiguity aversion, while leaving the fraction of participants classified as averse unchanged.

items.title: The Intersection of Dark Patterns and Cybersecurity
items.abstract: This chapter explores the intersection between dark patterns and cybersecurity, highlighting how manipulative interface designs contribute to emerging cyber threats. It outlines key mechanisms through which dark patterns exploit cognitive biases such as urgency, scarcity, and social proof, increasing user susceptibility to social engineering attacks. The chapter examines evolving threat vectors, including phishing, spoofed interfaces, malware delivery, and ClickFix-style attacks, which leverage deceptive user interface (UI) elements. It also discusses the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in amplifying both offensive and defensive cybersecurity strategies. Through analysis of recent threat trends, the chapter emphasizes the growing importance of human factors in security breaches. Finally, it addresses ethical, regulatory, and design-based mitigation strategies, advocating for transparent interfaces, user awareness, and integrated security frameworks to reduce risks and enhance trust in digital systems.

items.title: The leading role of technological factors in the development of the global online education market
items.abstract: The article analyzes the leading role of technological factors in the development of the global online education market. The impact of the spread of the Worldwide Web, mobile devices, cloud services, artificial intelligence, e-learning, personalization of learning, virtual and augmented reality, information security, big data, and gamification of learning on the transformation of the educational environment is considered. It is shown that digital technologies have accelerated the transition from traditional forms of education to online formats, expanded access to educational resources, and made learning more flexible, personalized, and scalable. Special attention is paid to how technological innovations are changing the models of interaction between students and educational platforms, improving the quality of content and creating new mechanisms for evaluating learning outcomes. The growth factors of the online education market are also considered, including the development of digital infrastructure, increasing the investment attractiveness of the EdTech sector and the growing demand for distance education services. The paper emphasizes that technological factors are not only a condition, but also the main driver of further expansion of the global online education market. It is concluded that the further development of this field will be determined by the speed of innovation and the ability of educational organizations to adapt to digital transformation.

items.title: The Next Generation of Power-grid Resilience: Long-horizon AI Planning under Deep Climate Uncertainty
items.abstract: Power systems face climate-driven extremes, compound hazards, rapid electrification and renewable integration, and infrastructure decisions whose consequences persist for decades. These conditions often cannot be represented by historical patterns or well-defined probability distributions. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to forecasting, outage prediction, asset management, optimisation and resilience planning, yet most applications remain prediction-centric, whereas long-horizon grid planning takes place under deep uncertainty. This critical narrative review integrates literature from power-systems engineering, machine learning, climate-risk assessment, infrastructure resilience and decision-making under deep uncertainty to examine how AI can move from forecasting toward robust and adaptive planning. We identify a prediction–planning gap created by two mismatches: a temporal mismatch between the horizons over which AI is predictively competent and those over which infrastructure decisions operate, and an uncertainty mismatch between the stationarity assumptions of learned models and the non-stationary, deeply uncertain conditions of future grids. Distribution shift, rare extremes, model disagreement and optimisation fragility limit prediction-centric approaches. AI offers greater long-term value through scenario exploration, surrogate-accelerated simulation, stress testing, vulnerability discovery, robust multi-objective optimisation and adaptive decision support. We operationalise this shift through an AI-Enabled Adaptive Resilience Planning Framework of six iterative stages, propose a decision-performance evaluation scheme (robustness, regret, adaptability, option value, recovery, equity and tail cost), and set out eight research priorities. Next-generation grid resilience should judge AI not by how accurately it predicts one future, but by how well it supports robust, equitable, explainable and adaptable decisions across many plausible futures.

items.title: The Orbital Mind: A Formal Research Program for Regulatory Conflict and Action Initiation
items.abstract: The Orbital Mind proposes that difficulties of self-regulation can arise from interactions among otherwise useful functions rather than a deficit in one function alone. This paper translates the book's formal research program into a more restricted, testable agenda. A mathematical audit separates properties of a proposed model from consequences that require additional assumptions: mutual inhibition does not guarantee a stable co-active deadlock; a threshold crossing need not be a fold bifurcation; and a generic recurrent network need not possess a scalar potential. A separately specified cubic normal form illustrates conditional predictions about action initiation, cessation and barrier height. Deterministic branch calculations and counterexamples are supplied as reproducible illustrations, not observations of human behavior. Ten hypotheses are organized into staged behavioral, measurement, neural and cross-scale studies. The first priority is a nonclinical action-initiation experiment with parameter and model recovery, matched alternatives, and held-out prediction. No participants, clinical outcomes, fitted psychological parameters or evidence of cross-scale invariance are reported. The contribution is a corrected mathematical specification and a prospective research agenda, not a validated theory of the self. Status: Theoretical and methodological working paper, version 1.0; not peer reviewed. No human participants, clinical results, fitted psychological parameters, preregistration or validation of cross-scale invariance are reported. Materials: The standalone LaTeX PDF is accompanied by the source, deterministic calculation code, 15,606 synthetic equilibrium-branch rows, mathematical checks, environment instructions and checksums. The illustrations do not simulate or validate human behavior. Companion book: The Orbital Mind: The Astrophysics of the Self, by Mayone Maha Rajan, The Maha Research Series, Book 2. Adapted from Part V and Appendices D–F of the October 2026 revised book. Kindle ebook; paperback (ISBN 9798161302286). The book provides conceptual provenance, not evidence validating the proposal. Purchasing the book is not necessary to understand or reproduce the paper. Disclosure: ChatGPT assisted the adaptation, literature checks, mathematical audit, code, drafting and typesetting. The author directs and takes responsibility for the release and has a commercial interest in the companion book. AI assistance is not independent expert review.

items.title: The prime frontier of the Yellowstone permutation falls behind time: limsup R(t)/t < 1
items.abstract: This manuscript continues the series on the Yellowstone permutation a (OEIS A098550). Let R(t) be the least odd prime with no multiple among a(1), ..., a(t), for a prime p let n_p be the first index with p | a(n_p), and let E(t) be the number of even terms among a(1), ..., a(t). The previous manuscript of the series proved R(t) <= (2.715 + o(1)) t. We prove that the prime frontier eventually falls behind time: limsup R(t)/t <= 0.9265 < 1, liminf n_p/p >= 1/0.9265 > 1.0793, and liminf E(t)/t >= 0.2440; hence, with the frontier corollary of Part II, a(n) <= max_{j<=n} a(j) <= (0.9265 + o(1)) n ln n. In particular the inequality a(n) <= (pi/2) n ln n of OEIS Conjecture 7 holds for all n >= n_0, where n_0 is ineffective. These constants use a smooth-part Rankin count for the masks, for which two independent proofs are given (Appendices A and B). With Rankin counts only, the same method gives limsup R(t)/t <= 1.045 < pi/2, liminf n_p/p > 0.9569 > 2/pi and liminf E(t)/t >= 0.2301, so liminf n_p/p > 1 is not reached by Rankin counts alone. On the way the manuscript proves the intermediate bounds on limsup R(t)/t: 2.405, 4.625/3, 1.2275, 1.215 and 1.155 (Rankin counts) and 2.14, 4.025/3, 1.1075, 1.08, 2.96/3 and 0.9625 (smooth-part count). The new ingredients are a hole sieve (an even number 2k still unused at time t forces every earlier step with an even anchor and a larger value to have a mask sharing an odd prime with k, by the closure lemma of Part I), the remark that a used odd value above the odd-mask level either has an odd mask or follows an even term, a low chain with a Rankin count at one fixed exponent, few-big-terms rates split by the parity of the mask, an elementary parity count that yields the lower bound on E(t), a split of the forced band at the entry of a prime, and a split of the times into classes according to E(t)/t. All thresholds are ineffective and the results are purely asymptotic; the numerics are double precision with outward-rounded discretisation, not interval arithmetic. Conjecture 7 for all n is NOT proved, no explicit n_0 is given, and a proof of liminf n_p/p >= 1 by Rankin counts alone, as well as the parity bound liminf E(t)/t >= 0.275 used by a conditional result of the program, remain open. items.title: The Profile of Graduate Theses On Occupational Health and Safety in The Healthcare Sector (1990-2024)
items.abstract: Health is one of the most fundamental human needs. Ensuring the occupational health and safety of healthcare workers is essential for the safe and effective delivery of healthcare services. This issue has been extensively addressed in graduate theses from various perspectives. To reveal the current state of literature and guide future research, this study examines graduate theses focusing on occupational health and safety in the healthcare sector, in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Accordingly, 555 graduate theses completed between 1990 and 2024 were included in this study were included. The theses included in the study were examined using content analyses. The theses were classified by considering various aspects, such as year of publication, thesis type, university, department, research topic, and research method used. The findings show that most theses were at the master’s level, their number increased steadily over time, and the highest output in the last five years was in 2022. While the theses were produced at 137 different universities, the highest number was produced at Beykent University within the Institute of Health Sciences and the Department of Health Management. Studies focusing on risk assessment and management were the most predominant. The findings of this study are expected to guide and motivate research on occupational health and safety in the healthcare sector.

items.title: The Psychology of Generative AI Dependence: Reward, PsychologicalNeeds, and the Emerging Architecture of Problematic Human–AIEngagement
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has transformed the relationship between humans and digital technology. Unlike digital systems that primarily delivered information, mediated interpersonal communication, or provided entertainment, generative AI can respond conversationally, personalise interactions, produce immediate solutions, simulate empathy, reduce cognitive effort, and remain continuously available. These characteristics raise an emerging question: can repeated engagement with generative AI develop into psychologically dependent or addiction-like patterns, and, if so, through what mechanisms? This paper employs an integrative critical literature review and conceptual synthesis to examine problematic generative-AI use through the combined perspectives of behavioural addiction theory, reward and reinforcement processes, the Interaction of Person–Affect–Cognition–Execution (I-PACE) model, self-determination theory, compensatory technology use, social anxiety, loneliness, anthropomorphism, cognitive offloading, and human psychological needs. The current study identifies a major gap in the current literature: emerging research frequently examines AI dependence as either a behavioural outcome, an educational problem, or a form of social attachment, but insufficiently integrates the neuropsychological processes of reinforcement with the psychological needs that make generative AI personally rewarding. To address this gap, this paper proposes the Need–Reward–Dependence (NRD) Framework, according to which problematic GenAI engagement develops through the interaction of three processes: unmet or salient psychological needs, rapid need-contingent reinforcement delivered by AI, and repeated cognitive or emotional outsourcing that strengthens habitual reliance. The framework proposes that competence, relatedness, autonomy, reassurance, emotional regulation, cognitive ease, social safety, and control can act as psychologically rewarding affordances of generative AI. Repeated reinforcement may increase cue-reactivity, habitual checking, perceived indispensability, cognitive delegation, emotional attachment, and impaired self-regulation in susceptible users. Importantly, this paper does not claim that generative-AI addiction is currently established as a distinct psychiatric disorder. Rather, it argues that a theoretically coherent and increasingly empirically observable continuum exists from adaptive use through reliance and dependence to potentially compulsive engagement associated with functional impairment. The paper concludes that future research should distinguish productive high-frequency use from clinically meaningful problematic use and should examine the interaction between users’ psychological vulnerabilities and the reward architecture of generative-AI systems

items.title: The REAL framework: evaluating the cognitive and formative impact of generative AI
items.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to address a gap in contemporary scholarship on generative artificial intelligence (AI) by shifting attention from the functional evaluation of AI systems to the formative impact of repeated AI use on the human user. It introduces formative evaluation as a complementary approach concerned with how sustained AI use may shape cognitive skills, habits, reasoning, judgment and agency over time. To address this concern, the paper proposes the REAL Framework (Retained, Eroded, Atrophied, Leveraged) as a practical means of evaluating and intentionally shaping patterns of AI use. Design/methodology/approach This conceptual paper develops the REAL Framework through interdisciplinary synthesis and theoretical analysis. It integrates scholarship on human agency and principal-agent relationships with research on cognitive offloading, cognitive reserve, desirable difficulty, automation bias and human–AI collaboration. Emerging empirical research on the cognitive effects of generative AI is used to contextualize and support the framework. The resulting four-dimensional framework is then illustrated through its application to professional practice and considered in relation to potential objections, limitations and directions for future empirical research. Findings The analysis identifies formative evaluation as a distinct and underdeveloped dimension of AI evaluation. While emerging research increasingly documents potential cognitive effects of generative AI use, practical means of evaluating and responding to those effects remain limited. The REAL Framework addresses this gap through four dimensions: Retained, Eroded, Atrophied and Leveraged. Together, these dimensions distinguish between AI use that preserves human agency and cognitive engagement, use that risks over-delegation and capability loss, and use that intentionally leverages AI to enhance human thinking and judgment. Research limitations/implications The REAL Framework is a conceptual and reflective framework that has not yet been empirically validated or operationalized as a measurement instrument. Longitudinal research is needed to examine the formative effects of sustained generative AI use and determine whether structured application of the framework influences patterns of AI delegation or preserves cognitive engagement and capability. Future research should develop and test measures associated with the framework’s four dimensions and examine their applicability across educational, professional and organizational contexts. Practical implications The REAL Framework provides individuals and institutions with a practical means of evaluating how generative AI is being incorporated into learning and professional practice. Its four reflective dimensions can help users identify inappropriate over-delegation, preserve important cognitive and professional capabilities, and redesign AI use to support rather than replace human reasoning and judgment. The framework may also inform institutional guidance, professional development and AI literacy initiatives by shifting attention from whether AI should be used toward how it can be used while preserving meaningful human agency and engagement. Social implications As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in education, work and everyday decision-making, its societal effects will depend not only on the capabilities of AI systems but also on how their use shapes human capabilities over time. The REAL Framework highlights the importance of preserving human agency, reasoning, judgment and cognitive engagement while benefiting from technological advancement. It encourages a broader societal conversation about which human capacities should remain meaningfully exercised and which may appropriately be delegated to increasingly capable AI systems. Originality/value This paper introduces formative evaluation as a distinct conceptual approach to understanding generative AI use, complementing prevailing functional approaches concerned primarily with AI systems, governance and responsible use. It advances the REAL Framework as a structured means of translating emerging concerns about AI’s cognitive and formative effects into reflective practice. By connecting human agency and delegation with cognitive development, the framework shifts attention from evaluating what AI can do to evaluating what repeated AI use may be doing to the human user.

items.title: The rebirth of the author: writing critical social theory in the time of generative AI
items.abstract: Abstract Sociologists face the pressing question of how large language model-based technologies can contribute to social theorising. Several social scientists have called for a greater integration of generative AI tools in the social sciences and humanities to speed and scale up the production of social theory. In this article, we adopt a more cautious approach, reflecting on how the adoption of generative AI raises foundational questions about the construction, refinement and evaluation of critical social theory. To make this argument, we create and critically analyse a speculative piece of dystopian sociological fiction. This enables us to explore the values and practices of critical social theory authorship. We argue that authorship must be ‘recentred’, particularly with regard to four key values of authorial practice: (1) standpoint, (2) creativity, (3) pluralism and (4) accountability. In the present moment, the use of generative AI as substitution for authorial practices redefines and potentially threatens authorship in ways that problematises its particular use in generating critical social theory. With regards to standpoint, generative AI technologies run the risk of reproducing an ‘abstract masculinity’ that feminist scholars have long written against. The relational wonder at the heart of social theory creativity is undermined by generative AI use, as is the pluralism of creativity. Generative AI also flattens and overlooks pluralism of voice, as well as dilutes authorial accountability. We sociologists need to defend and rearticulate what we contribute to social theory and its concomitant politics, both in the theories themselves and in the project of social theorising. It is with this in mind that we call for the ‘rebirth’ - that is, the recentralisation - of the human author in critical social theory creation.

items.title: The Review on Smart Companion Robot for People with Intellectual Disabilities and Epilepsy
items.abstract: People with intellectual disabilities who experience epilepsy may require additional support for daily activities, seizure monitoring and emergency communication. Recent developments in artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML) and assistive robotics offer opportunities to improve safety and caregiver support. This study reviews the supplied research papers on automated seizure detection, AI-based epilepsy monitoring and assistive technologies for people with disabilities. Zhu et al. (2024) proposed a hybrid SE-TCN-BiGRU network and reported high seizure-detection accuracy on the CHB-MIT and SH-SDU datasets. Garção et al. (2025) Developed a video-based approach for detecting seizures in real time using Lampsy, a non-intrusive monitoring solution powered by affordable edge devices. Research on assistive robotics highlights the potential of robots to support rehabilitation and interaction, while Milne-Ives et al. (2025) emphasised the underrepresentation of People with intellectual impairments participating in artificial intelligence research on epilepsy. Based on these findings, this study proposes a smart robotic assistant designed to support daily living through voice interaction, scheduled alerts, and seizure-event tracking. and caregiver notifications. The proposed system aims to provide personalised assistance through accessible interaction, privacy-conscious monitoring and human supervision. However, existing studies evaluate individual technologies rather than the complete proposed robot. Therefore, its effectiveness, usability and reliability cannot yet be assumed. Further development, user-centred testing and appropriate clinical evaluation are necessary to assess its practical benefits and safety. This study explores potential advancements and existing limitations in integrating intelligent seizure monitoring with socially assistive robotics to support people with intellectual disabilities and epilepsy.

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Enhancing Predictive Maintenance in Smart Industrial Robotics
items.abstract: Predictive Maintenance (PdM) is the model that brings together sensor data as well as systematic data analysis. Industry 4.0 is broadly using PdMs that are improving the applications of digitized information. The monitoring of the conditions of machine parts and various processes is the main goal of PdM because it predicts the occurrence of any possible failures and results in interventions to optimized maintenance. Nevertheless, rotational components employed in robotics are very important in terms of proactive maintenance. The applications of machine learning models to obtain real-time data and predict when a failure may occur long before the breakdown were the subject of our study. The predictive models are highly accurate on possible component malfunctions with a very reasonable accuracy. Random Forest offers a good accuracy of 92% whereas Neural Network model offers a better accuracy of 94%. These models are efficient as evidenced by their performance measures including precision, recall and the F1-score. These indicators focus on the capability of the model to identify timely component failures.

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Modern Business Management: A Conceptual Study of Opportunities and Challenges
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from the periphery of experimental computing to the centre of managerial practice, reshaping how organisations make decisions, allocate resources, engage customers and manage people. Despite the rapid growth of scholarship on the subject, the literature remains fragmented across functional silos, and the opportunities and risks of AI are frequently examined in isolation from one another. This conceptual study synthesises existing literature to examine the role of AI in modern business management and to articulate an integrated understanding of its opportunities and challenges. Drawing on the technology–organisation–environment framework, the resource-based view, dynamic capabilities theory and the automation–augmentation perspective, the paper develops a conceptual model comprising five interrelated components: AI adoption enablers, AI applications across management functions, the dual effects of AI (opportunities and challenges), organisational outcomes, and moderating governance mechanisms. The model proposes that AI generates sustainable value only when technological capability is matched by organisational readiness, responsible governance, effective human–AI collaboration and continuous workforce development. The discussion elaborates the implications of the model for strategic decision-making, operations, marketing, human resource management and finance, and considers the ethical, social and implementation challenges that accompany adoption. The paper contributes a theoretically grounded and integrative framework that can guide future empirical research and support managers who seek to adopt AI responsibly and effectively.

items.title: The Twin Transition and Labor Market Transformation: A Conceptual Framework for AI-Enabled Green Growth
items.abstract: The green and digital transitions do not automatically produce inclusive growth. They interact through distinct labour-market processes: green structural change reallocates employment across sectors and places, whereas artificial intelligence (AI) reorganises tasks and authority within workplaces. This article develops a process-based conceptual framework for examining when their interaction can support AI-enabled green growth. An integrative review brings together peer-reviewed research and recent comparative reports. The framework follows a directional sequence in which green restructuring and AI deployment generate sectoral reallocation and task/workplace reorganisation. Labour-market adjustment arrangements and structural context then shape how these mechanisms lead to environmental, productivity, employment, job-quality, and distributive outcomes. These elements are not specified as independent, dependent, mediator, or moderator variables because the article does not estimate a statistical model. The framework distinguishes an enabling pathway based on labour augmentation and shared productivity gains from an adverse pathway involving displacement, surveillance, unequal value capture, and ecological externalisation. Six propositions identify relationships for subsequent empirical examination. A renewable-electricity value-chain application illustrates why AI exposure and labour effects differ across manufacturing, construction, and operations. The contribution is a power-sensitive account that treats environmental improvement and decent work as joint and institutionally contingent outcomes.Keywords: twin transition, artificial intelligence, labour-market adaptation, just transition, green growth.

items.title: The Ultimate Guide to AI Agent Security and Sandboxing
items.abstract: Abstract The "Provisional specification.pdf" introduces a comprehensive security architecture for governing autonomous artificial intelligence agents across isolated runtimes, administrative domains, and hardware environments. As AI agents increasingly invoke external tools and modify persistent data, the system distinguishes between an agent's ability to compute and its authority to execute consequential external effects. The architecture intercepts proposed agent operations, holding them in a non-effective state while a protected enforcement domain evaluates operation-specific authorization conditions and commits validation evidence. items.abstract: This manuscript continues the series on the Yellowstone permutation a (OEIS A098550). Let R(t) be the least odd prime with no multiple among a(1), ..., a(t), for a prime p let n_p be the first index with p | a(n_p), let M(n) = max_{j<=n} a(j), and let E(t) be the number of even terms among a(1), ..., a(t). items.title: Theoretical, Legal and Strategic Foundations of Counterintelligence in the United States of America as Benchmarks for Transforming Ukrainian Counterintelligence
items.abstract: This article analyzes the current organization of counterintelligence in the United States. In today’s evolving security environment, characterized by globalization and multidimensional threats, counterintelligence has become a vital tool for protecting fundamental state interests. Ukraine is currently fighting a war against Russia while simultaneously standing at the center of a global geopolitical confrontation. Therefore, studying the American counterintelligence model and adopting its best practices is crucial for strengthening Ukraine’s national security. The study highlights that the United States lacks both a single consolidated law governing counterintelligence and a unified agency to conduct it. Instead, the American model is highly diversified and extraterritorial. The Director of National Intelligence coordinates these efforts under the guidance of the US President. Particular attention is given to the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency, which plays a pivotal role in ensuring personnel, industrial, and technological security. A significant portion of the research analyzes the current US National Counterintelligence Strategy (2024–2027), noting a substantial expansion of what requires counterintelligence protection. Beyond traditional government institutions, US counterintelligence now focuses on safeguarding advanced technologies, the national innovation base, large datasets, and critical supply chains. Furthermore, it actively protects the integrity of society and democratic institutions against the threat of informational influence campaigns. Based on the study’s findings, the author has formulated 16 initiatives to improve the effectiveness of Ukraine’s counterintelligence. It is proposed to expand the goals and objectives of counterintelligence and to adopt a Counterintelligence Strategy for Ukraine. It is recommended that the Security Service of Ukraine should be assigned additional counterintelligence functions related to the protection of domestic cutting-edge technologies and innovations, as well as supply chains; the assessment of the reliability of private companies fulfilling defense contracts; monitoring individuals with security clearances; and annually informing the public about the status and trends in threats to Ukraine’s national interests in the field of state security. Furthermore, the author suggests delineating offensive and defensive counterintelligence measures at the legislative level. It is also necessary to regulate the use of artificial intelligence in this field and strengthen the institutional capacity of prosecutors to oversee the legal compliance of domestic intelligence agencies. Finally, to safeguard human rights and freedoms, the article advocates for establishing robust parliamentary oversight by creating the position of a Special Representative of the Ukrainian Ombudsman.

items.title: Third Eye: AI and IoT-Based Smart Navigation and Safety Sys-tem for Visually Impaired People — A Comprehensive Review
items.abstract: Visual impairment restricts independent mobility and exposes people to collisions, falls and unsafe road situations. White canes and guide dogs remain the main aids, but they give little information about what an obstacle is, how far away it is, or when the user needs help. Artificial intelligence (AI) combined with wearable sensing and the Internet of Things (IoT) is increasingly proposed as a route to smart navigation and safety systems that perceive the scene, guide the user by audio or touch, and alert caregivers in an emergency. This paper presents a focused narrative review of five verified studies, published between 2018 and 2026 in IEEE, MDPI and River Publishers outlets, that cover sensor-based safety alerting, RGB-D and deep-learning navigation, machine-learning smart cane and glasses, edge-TPU indoor navigation, and an AIoT eyewear system with LiDAR ranging and an SOS function. The review examines sensing, AI perception, feedback and IoT integration. The literature shows that recent systems report object-detection accuracy of about 95 % and centimetre-level distance error in controlled tests, and that low-cost edge hardware such as the Raspberry Pi with a Google Coral TPU can run navigation models on the wearable itself. However, evidence is dominated by small prototypes, controlled or indoor settings, heterogeneous metrics and limited testing with visually impaired users, and few systems join navigation, perception and caregiver-facing safety in one design. The paper contributes a comparative analysis of the studies, a proposed conceptual “Third Eye” architecture that links wearable sensing, edge AI, IoT safety alerts and field validation, and a prioritised agenda of research gaps and directions.

items.title: Towards a world-centred AI literacy in middle school education? Reflections from a Swedish case
items.abstract: With artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly influencing children’s and youth’s lives, AI literacy has been promoted as an educational concern at all levels of schooling. While AI literacy initiatives are being introduced globally, the specific components and the objectives of this literacy remain undecided. This position paper challenges the current discourse of AI literacy by drawing attention to multiple purposes of AI literacy in middle school education that may co-exist and collide. We do so by applying Biesta’s world-centred education framework as an analytical lens, and by grounding the argument in classroom observations and interviews with middle school students. Our findings highlight both tensions and overlaps between middle school students’ often vague and fragmented formal knowledge and skills (qualification) of what AI is and how it works, and their more developed reflections related to norms and ethical concerns (socialisation), as well as agency (subjectification). We suggest that for AI literacy to truly empower students, both curriculum design and professional development must account for a broad spectrum of educational goals.

items.abstract: ToxPipe is a modular, fully open-source software stack designed to accelerate toxicological data analysis and decision-making by integrating large language model (LLM) capabilities with workflow, monitoring, and user-interface services. ToxPipe leverages existing open-source technologies like LibreChat, LiteLLM, and Langflow to provide centralized and streamlined access to different LLMs for end users and developers and logging and auditing of LLM use for organizations. ToxPipe also allows for open-source/local model support. While the ToxPipe ecosystem also supports advanced AI functions such as MCP server integration, RAG and literature search, and agent creation, we did not observe clear benefits using these configurations relative to the GPT-5.5 baseline assertion coverage scores. ToxPipe is available as a series of Docker containers for rapid and reproducible deployment.

items.title: Transcending the Weberian Paradox: Fluid Institutions, Agentic Artificial Intelligence, and the Evolution of Post-Bureaucratic State Systems
items.abstract: The modern democratic state is characterised by a structural anomaly that has long confounded political sociology and institutional theory: populations of advanced, highly complex societies live under the continuous, dense administration of unelected specialists, yet they periodically delegate supreme formal authority to a single individual selected on the basis of campaign performance and diffuse public trust. Max Weber diagnosed this condition, recognising the permanent, rationalised bureaucracy as the most efficient and indestructible organisational form in human history, while warning of its tendency to become an "iron cage" devoid of ultimate values. To prevent this, he prescribed the charismatic leader, empowered by plebiscitary democracy, who would supply the state with ends and hold the experts in check. This article argues, following Berkovski (2026), that the remedy is itself a paradox: the more specialised the administrative machine, the more the leader depends on the bureaucracy's monopoly over knowledge. Berkovski's Oakeshottian alternative — officialdom checked by rival officialdom — is sound but remains analog, slow and exposed to ossification, capture and the Schmittian critique of liberal parliamentarianism. Drawing on polycentric governance, agile public administration and agentic artificial intelligence, the article proposes a framework of fluid institutions organised on Adaptive, Agentic and Agile (AAA) principles. It maps Ostrom's eight design principles onto algorithmic governance, confronts the documented failures of automated administration, and concludes that the structural permanence of bureaucracy is no longer an insurmountable precondition of state capacity, provided that files are kept open, algorithms auditable and human accountability intact. Subtitle: Knowledge monopolies, plural checking and the Adaptive, Agentic and Agile state. Companion to the anatomical review of Berkovski (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23577500).

items.title: Transforming Digital Forensics with Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: The intersection of AI and digital forensics symbolizes the paradigm shift in criminal investigation and protection against cybercrimes. The chapter discusses the ways in which AI technologies will radically change the process of forensic practices, making it faster, more accurate, and comprehensive when analyzing digital evidence. The combination of machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and computer vision with the forensic workflow has created unprecedented opportunities regarding the processing of large amounts of digital data, detecting intricate trends, and automating formerly labor-intensive aspects of the investigation process. Modern forensic investigations are witnessing a geometric increase in the volumes of data available to them, in multiple forms such as IoT-based devices, social media platforms, encrypted communications, and advanced vectors of cyberattacks. The intelligent automation, predictive analytics, and adaptive learning mechanisms are AI-based solutions to these problems. Nevertheless, this technological development presents urgent concerns about interpretability, bias, privacy, and admissibility in court. The chapter discusses the theoretical background, its practical use, transformative advantages, and ongoing issues, as well as the future directions of AI-enabled digital forensics, in a thorough analysis of how intelligent systems are changing the face of forensic science and criminal justice.

items.title: Transforming Global Early Childhood Education Through Artificial Intelligence: Addressing Teacher Shortages, Inequality, and Quality Gaps in Early Learning Systems
items.abstract: This study examines the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) to support early childhood education (ECE) in addressing workforce pressures, inequality, and quality-related challenges, while identifying the organisational, pedagogical, and ethical conditions required for responsible AI use. An interpretivist qualitative design was used with 22 participants (8 head teachers and 14 early childhood teachers) from ECE institutions in Sydney, Australia, who took part in semi-structured face-to-face interviews. Six interconnected themes emerged from inductive thematic analysis: workforce and operational challenges; AI awareness and readiness; AI as teacher support, not replacement; AI and equity; AI and learning quality; and responsible AI adoption. Participants considered how AI could support planning, documentation, translation, administration, and personalised learning, freeing up time for meaningful teacher–child interaction. They stressed, however, that AI cannot address structural workforce shortages and cannot take the place of teachers’ relational, professional, and safeguarding roles. The study’s contribution lies in bringing together workforce, equity, learn-ing quality, and responsible AI adoption within a single ECE-focused empirical framework, and in highlighting the necessity of human-centred implementation. Longitudinal and mixed-methods studies in various settings are needed to inves-tigate the impact of AI on teacher workload, child outcomes, equity, and policy implementation.
